Article Title: ‘Reading the batter’s mind’: How batting all-rounder Naman Dhir turned his bowling into a weapon for India
Article Text:
Naman Dhir celebrates after taking a wicket. (PTI Photo)

‘He was looking to play every shot towards the leg side’

Batting remains Dhir’s primary role

NEW DELHI: India’s Naman Dhir is making an impact with the ball despite being primarily a batting all-rounder, and the 26-year-old believes his ability to read a batter’s intentions is helping him deliver crucial breakthroughs in T20Is.Dhir claimed two wickets (2/39) in India’s 14-run victory over the West Indies in the third T20I at the Holkar Stadium in Indore on Sunday, helping the hosts take a 2-1 lead in the five-match series. The off-spinner dismissed Shimron Hetmyer and Kamil Pooran during the visitors’ chase of 224, adding to the three wickets (3/31) he took on his T20I debut during the West Indies series.Explaining his approach, Dhir said his bowling relies on disciplined lines and lengths, variations in pace and an understanding of the batter’s technique.“As an off-spinner, I don’t have too many variations, so I have to rely on my line and length and vary my pace. That has always been my thinking. As they say that in T20 cricket, an attacking option can also be a defensive option because there is nothing better than taking a wicket,” Dhir told JioStar.“It helps being a batter because you understand the batter’s stance, where his backlift is coming from, his guard and the kind of shots he can play.I keep observing these things when I bowl,” he added.Dhir offered an insight into how he planned the dismissal of Pooran, explaining that he had identified the batter’s preferred scoring areas and wanted to restrict his room to play freely.“I didn’t plan to concede three sixes and then take a wicket. For instance, when Kamil Pooran was batting, he was looking to play every shot towards the leg side and get room to free his arms, so I wanted to cramp him for room,” he said.“I made a couple of errors in the first two deliveries. I knew I was bowling my third over, the batter was set, and with the run rate being high, he was bound to take a chance. And, ultimately, he got out playing exactly the kind of shot I wanted him to, getting caught at square-leg.”“So, these little things help me a lot, and as a bowler, I keep looking for such small details,” Dhir added.Despite his growing contributions with the ball, Dhir made it clear that batting remains his primary responsibility in the Indian setup. He said the team management expects him to provide flexibility in the lower middle order while delivering two or three overs when required.“I am a batting all-rounder. I got an opportunity to bat in this game, but I am a bit disappointed that I couldn’t capitalise on it,” he said.Dhir added that the Impact Player rule in the IPL had reduced his bowling opportunities, but stressed that bowling had always been part of his game.“With the ball, my responsibility is to bowl two or three overs economically whenever the team needs me,” he said.The all-rounder is not looking too far ahead despite his promising start to international cricket.“I don’t function that way, by looking too far ahead. I don’t have any specific goals as of now. I’m just playing my cricket, enjoying it, and wherever God takes me, I’ll go,” he added.
Article Summary: Naman Dhir claims two wickets in India’s 14-run victory over the West Indies in the third T20I at the Holkar Stadium in Indore on Sunday. The off-spinner dismissed Shimron Hetmyer and Kamil Pooran during the visitors’ chase of 224. Dhir made it clear that batting remains his primary responsibility in the Indian setup.

Article Text:

MUMBAI: Former India captain Dilip Vengsarkar has criticised the BCCI ’s decision to send an India A team on a shadow tour of New Zealand during the 2026-27 Ranji Trophy season.A 15-member India A squad, led by wicketkeeper-batter Dhruv Jurel, will tour New Zealand for three four-day matches in Lincoln and Christchurch from Oct 24 to Nov 7, ahead of India’s two-Test series there.“Why do you have an India A tour when the Ranji Trophy season is in progress? What’s the point of holding the Ranji Trophy then?” Vengsarkar told TOI.“This idea of having a shadow tour when your own domestic season is on is plain ridiculous because you are diluting the importance of your premier domestic tournament.”Most players picked for the India A tour are likely to feature in only the opening round of the Ranji Trophy before leaving for New Zealand.“If your best domestic players are playing for India A during the Ranji Trophy, then performances of those who score runs and take wickets in the Ranji Trophy get devalued,” said Vengsarkar, a former India chief selector.“It’s beyond me why these A tours are being organised during the domestic season.”Vengsarkar has previously questioned the BCCI’s scheduling of India A tours and home series during the domestic calendar.This season, the Irani Cup between 2025-26 Ranji Trophy champions Jammu & Kashmir and Rest of India also lost some sheen as IndiaA were simultaneously playing Australia A in two multi-day matches in Puducherry.The opening round of the Ranji Trophy has also clashed with the three-match one-day series between India A and Australia A.The BCCI introduced shadow tours to help fringe players get used to overseas conditions before the senior team’s assignment, ensuring ready reserves if required.Vengsarkar, however, does not agree with the logic.“If you want your players to acclimatise early to the conditions and local environment, then send your main team early,” the 116-Test veteran said.“There’s no point sending players who are not even going to play in the Test series.”
Article Summary: Dilip Vengsarkar has criticised the BCCI for sending an India A team on a shadow tour of New Zealand during the 2026-27 Ranji Trophy season. A 15-member India A squad, led by wicketkeeper-batter Dhruv Jurel, will tour New Zealand for three four-day matches in Lincoln and Christchurch from Oct 24 to Nov 7.

Article Title: Udhayveer Sidhu strikes gold at World Cup, opens India's senior medal account in Cairo
Article Text:
Udhayveer Sidhu

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

PUNE: A bout of anxiety, a Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan mood-lifter and gold. This is how Udhayveer Sidhu describes his journey traversed to his maiden World Cup gold as the Chandigarh shooter topped the podium in men’s 10m air pistol event at the ISSF World Cup in Cairo on Sunday.Udhayveer, 24, won his first senior and a World Cup medal, after shooting 240.6 in the final. He beat Rio Games gold medallist and veteran Christian Reitz of Germany (240.1) and Paris Games bronze medallist Paolo Monna of Italy (219.8) for silver and bronze, respectively. Paris Games 10m pistol mixed event silver medallist Yusuf Dikec finished seventh.“It was a good match to win. It was my first World Cup medal and a gold, so I am happy with the result. It was more special as it came against three Olympic medallists, including the great Christian Reitz, who we have grown up watching,” Udhayveer told TOI.Udhayveer had a successful juniors’ phase, as he had won three World Championships golds, however, his transition to the seniors wasn’t very smooth.He had shot in his first international tournament (Olympic event) in Munich World Cup earlier this year, where he finished 37th.“It was a difficult phase. Like any struggling athlete, I also had my lows and that brought in some self-doubts and frustrations. But I feel that is part of any athlete’s life. I tried to stay positive and keep doing my things,” Udhayveer said.The shooter admitted that he was anxious about the match. “I was nervous and anxious the last night. But then I put on some music, listened to my favourite qawwalis by Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan and calmed myself before the match. During the match, I was not nervous,” he said.Udhayveer was struggling in fourth position till the 12th shot. He started climbing up with the 13th shot, a 10.6. Monna was still leading with consistent high 10s. The Indian took second spot after the 14th shot, leaving Reitz behind by 0.3 point. After making his place in the medals slot, Udhayveer kept it around 10, while Reitz and Monna shot 9s and 8s.Udhayveer’s consistency paid off after the 21st and 22nd shots when Monna hit a 9.9 and 8.9, while the Indian shot 10 and 9.8 to take the lead. Monna got the bronze.Udhayveer shot 585 in the qualification round. Ajendra Singh Chauhan (14th with 580) and Paris Games mixed event bronze medallist Sarabjot Singh (31st with 574) were far below.
Article Summary: Udhayveer Sidhu won his first senior and a World Cup medal, after shooting 240.6 in the final. He beat Rio Games gold medallist and veteran Christian Reitz of Germany (240.1) and Paolo Monna of Italy (219.8) for silver and bronze.

Article Title: Russia hand India another reality check, win 8-0
Article Text:
India vs Russia (Pic credit: AIFF)

KOLKATA: India head coach Crispin Chettri was seen making a solemn gesture of disappointment on the touchline when Darina Ishmukhametova gave Russia the breakthrough in the 22nd minute at Kishore Bharati Krirangan here on Sunday.Despite Russia head coach Yuri Krasnozhan retaining only two players from the starting line-up that secured a 4-0 win in the first friendly on Thursday, the visitors once again showcased their class and quality, beating hosts India 8-0 in the second ‘unofficial’ international match.For the opening 21 minutes, the Indians virtually parked the bus in their own half and managed to keep the relentless Russian attacks at bay, thanks largely to some determined defending, especially from Ranjana Chanu. However, Ksenia Dolgova sent in a cross from the left that goalkeeper Monalisha Devi Moirangthem failed to hold on to, and Darina was on hand to tap home.The opener, as Chettri seemed to have anticipated, opened the floodgates as the world No. 27 side pumped in four more goals before half-time, much to the frustration of the sparse crowd supporting the hosts.While Marine Acholan (25th, 45+1) scored a quick brace, Diana Kishmakhova (30th) added another before Darina completed her brace with a penalty in the 42nd minute.Chettri did what he could, making tactical adjustments and substitutions across the field, bringing on Nandini in goal, Jasoda Munda in midfield, and pairing Babysana Devi with Lynda Kom Serto up front.However, it was a substitution made by Russia coach Krasnozhan that had the biggest impact. Star striker Natalia Mashina, who plays in the Turkish Women’s Super League, came on and scored twice in two minutes (49th, 51st) to restart the rout.There were, however, some positives from the Indian substitutions. Nandini showed glimpses of her ability with a few crucial saves, while the players displayed greater intent in venturing into the Russian half.
Article Summary: Darina Ishmukhametova gave Russia the breakthrough in the 22nd minute at Kishore Bharati Krirangan. Marine Acholan (25th, 45+1) scored a quick brace, Diana Kishmakhova (30th) added another before Darina completed her brace with a penalty in the 42nd minute. Star striker Natalia Mashina came on and scored twice in two minutes (49th, 51st) to restart the rout.

Article Title: Ranji Trophy: Karan Lamba hits unbeaten ton as Rajasthan batters make Tamil Nadu toil on a flat deck
Article Text:
Karan Lamba (TOI Photo)

Sai Sudharsan joins TN squad

Brief Scores:

JAIPUR: Sidelined for the last couple of years despite scoring a hundred on debut, Karan Lamba relaunched himself in style with a brilliant unbeaten century to provide Rajasthan a strong start against Tamil Nadu in the Ranji Trophy opener at the Sawai Mansingh Stadium here on Sunday.Karan, who last played Ranji tie in 2024, proved a point or two to his detractors by slamming his second ton of his career as Rajasthan reached 286 for 4 on Day 1.The opening day belonged to two former U-23 teammates – Karan and debutant Rohan Rajbhar. While the latter struck an undefeated 103 (133balls, 11x4, 1x6), the former missed the hundred by a whisker by falling on 95 on his first-class debut.At stumps, vice-captain Mahipal Lomror was giving Karan company on 31 off 48 balls (5x4) as visitors toiled hard throughout the day on a placid track.For Tamil Nadu medium-pacer Saravana Kumar, it was a day to remember. The 37-year-old, who made his First-Class debut in 2022 and last played in 2025, finished the day with 3-52. With not much on offer, the paceman’s work-ethic stood out as he bowled 19 overs through the day and got one each in every session.Captaining the Rajasthan side for the first time in Ranji, Manav Suthar won the toss and did not hesitate to bat first.Rajasthan lost opener Sachin Yadav (1) quite cheaply as Saravana Kumar trapped him on the first ball of his spell.Sumit Godara joined in the second over of the day and steadied the ship with Rohan with a solid 104-run stand to deny the visitors any further advantage.At lunch Rajasthan were strongly placed 100-1. Godara, who was batting on 49 at the break, did not add anything to his score and was dismissed in the fourth over in the post-lunch session.Karan was off the mark in style and dealt mostly in boundaries. The young duo of Rohan and Karan shared a 125-run stand for the third wicket before the visitors’ 37-year-old seamer Saravana snuffed out Rohan. His short ball kissed the opener’s gloves before landing in the safe hands of wicketkeeper N Jagadeesan.Trying to clear the mid-wicket fence, Kartik Sharma threw his wicket away to Washington Sundar, giving the visitors hope.However, Karan gelled well with Mahipal to restore the home team’s advantage.Having waited since Feb 2024 for a Ranji game, Karan did not look at his knock as a fitting answer to selectors. He said he just did what he needed to.“I have to do my job. Performing is in my hands, I focus on that. I don’t fret over selection too much; for me it’s all about how I can improve my game,” said Karan.Karan, who brought up his second FC century with a backfoot square drive for four off Saravana, admitted that the flat track helped his cause. “The wicket was good to bat on. You rarely get such flat tracks, so I made sure to cash in,” he said.Besides being teammates in the U-23 team last year, Rohan and Karan have both represented Jaipur at the district level and that helped their partnership.“It helped our running between the wickets. Having played together for a long time, we don’t usually have misunderstandings,” the 21-year-old said.“You can get selected from anywhere. It’s not that they will only pick from Ranji Trophy. If you perform well at the U-23s, they have their eyes on you anyway,” added Karan.Though Sunday’s ton came after two years of wait, Karan enjoyed his century on Ranji debut in 2023 against Jharkhand in Jaipur more. “As a cricketer, it is a dream to play in the Ranji Trophy. The day I realised that dream I hit a hundred so that was more satisfying,” he said.Catching everybody by surprise, Sai Sudharsan joins the TN squad to boost the batting line-up.“Sai came at 10pm on Saturday night from Puducherry. We didn't know about his arrival until he landed at the hotel,” said TN team manager Goutham Dangi.Rajasthan 286/4 in 85 overs (Karan Lamba 103*, Rohan Rajbhar 95, Sumit Godara 49, Mahipal Lomror 31*; Saravana Kumar 3-52, Washington Sundar 1-49).
Article Summary: Karan Lamba hits unbeaten 103 as Rajasthan reach 286 for 4 on Day 1. Sri Lanka's Sai Sudharsan joins the TN squad to boost the batting batting line-up. Tamil Nadu medium-pacer Saravana Kumar takes 3-52.

SA20 auction 2026 : Time and where to watch

The SA20 Season 5 Player Auction will take place on Wednesday, with four franchises set to fill 19 remaining slots and a combined $2.10 million available to spend.Durban’s Super Giants and Paarl Royals have already completed their squad-building after the league increased the salary cap to $2.54 million for the upcoming season.Among the four teams heading into the auction, Joburg Super Kings have the biggest purse with $1.245 million available. MI Cape Town have $565,150, Sunrisers Eastern Cape have $217,600, while Pretoria Capitals have just $89,150 remaining.Joburg Super Kings and MI Cape Town must each sign one Under-23 player from the final shortlist of 48 players. Joburg also have a wildcard slot still available.There will be no Right to Match cards at the Season 5 auction.Each team must have 19 players in its registered squad, comprising 18 regular squad members and one wildcard player.The 18-player squad can have a maximum of seven overseas players and must include at least 11 South African players, with two of those required to be Under-23 players.The wildcard can be either a South African or overseas player and will not count towards the salary cap.The auction will feature marquee mixed-set rounds followed by a nomination express round, in which teams can call up the player they want to bid for.The auction takes place on October 7, with SA20 Season 5 following a previous edition in which Dewald Brevis became the league's most expensive player after Pretoria Capitals bought him for R16.5 million.Matthew Breetzke is another player whose auction value has risen significantly. Durban’s Super Giants initially signed him for his base price of $10,576 at the inaugural auction before Sunrisers Eastern Cape bought him for $368,000 three seasons later.The Season 5 Player Auction begins at 8:30pm IST on Wednesday, October 7.In India, the auction will be broadcast on JioHotstar. It will also be streamed live on the official SA20 YouTube channel.
Article Summary: Joburg Super Kings have the biggest purse with $1.245 million available. MI Cape Town have $565,150, Sunrisers Eastern Cape have $217,600, while Pretoria Capitals have just $89,150 remaining. Joburg and MI must each sign one Under-23 player from the final shortlist of 48 players.

Article Title: ‘We’re not trying to be any other league’: SA20 COO Lynn Naudé on the league’s rapid rise
Article Text:
Lynn Naudé (left), COO of SA20 (Special Arrangement)

Excerpts

SA20 has grown rapidly in four seasons. What has been the biggest lesson behind that success?

How do you keep SA20 distinct in an increasingly crowded global T20 calendar?

What role has the league played in strengthening South African cricket beyond the professional level?

With overseas leagues expanding, how do you ensure SA20 continues attracting elite international players?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Looking ahead to Season 5, what is the one area where you want fans to notice a clear step forward?

NEW DELHI: Four seasons into its existence, SA20 has already established itself as one of the most prominent T20 leagues outside the IPL. But for COO Lynn Naudé, the league’s rapid rise has been less about chasing quick wins and more about getting the fundamentals right. From securing a prime South African summer window and putting Proteas at the heart of the competition to creating a strong match-day atmosphere, Naudé explains how SA20 has built its identity and what lies ahead in Season 5.I think probably the biggest lesson is that strong foundations matter more than quick wins. From the very start, we were very single-minded about what we believed success looked like. The fan experience, the quality of cricket and putting South African players at the heart of the competition were all important to us. We wanted to make sure SA20 felt like it belonged to South African fans as a starting point, and then we could take it global from there.I think that's probably been one of my biggest learnings. If you can get your basics right, the rest will follow from thereT20 cricket has got a unique feeling to it, and that's possibly a common thread. But I think there are a couple of things that have helped us.First, our window and our ability to secure it in the heart of the South African summer, with great conditions and full stadiums, was a real coup for us.That time of year lends itself to delivering a product that speaks very much to the fans, but also provides a fantastic experience both on broadcast and in the stadium.The second is the quality of the competition. The commitment from Cricket South Africa to make all of its Proteas available to play in the tournament season after season, and to see them compete with the best in the world, means that we have intentionally put cricket at the heart of the product.The third is probably the atmosphere at the venues. I think that's become something quite synonymous with SA20.If I had to wrap it up, I'd say we're not trying to be any other league. We're just trying to be the best version of SA20 that we can be.”It has actually been on multiple levels. The intention was for SA20 to almost become a bastion for South African cricket. There was obviously work that needed to be done to strengthen the talent pipeline.But outside of that, if I look back again on the last five seasons, it's also about the quality of the broadcast, what's improved in terms of the fan experience within the South African sporting context, our venues, the ways of working and how they operate on a day-to-day basis.There's also been a lot of knowledge transfer from SA20 into the greater cricket ecosystem, with some of the standards and expectations that we have for the type of product we want to deliver.We've had the opportunity to expose a lot of young talent in the sporting industry to our ways of working and the culture at SA20.In the lead-up to the 2027 World Cup, what we've tried to do is make sure that the cricket ecosystem, and those who deliver not only on the field but also off it, is better off the back of SA20 and the experience it has brought to the South African cricket landscape.At the highest level, elite players want to play where the cricket is competitive, the conditions are good and the environment is professional. I think that's something we strive to offer, and I think we do offer all three.Our franchises bring global experience and know how to run teams. The players know that when they come here, they'll be tested against strong domestic talent and they'll be playing in front of full stadiums.It's always surprising to me, anecdotally, when I hear players talk about how important it is to them to play in front of a crowd and how different it feels. I guess when you're talented like that, you feel appreciated when you're playing in front of a lot of people.That, coupled with the strong and stable franchise ownership groups that we've got, who invest in those players, offers them opportunities.If you have the opportunity to play in the SA20, you also have the opportunity to play in many other places around the world. I think consistency across all of those things will make sure that we remain attractive to players.Every season we run a fan survey, and it directly shapes what we deliver. Our fans have told us what they want to see more of, and they've also told us what they don't want us to change. Those are the types of things that shape our decisions.Our brand positioning at SA20 is ‘for everyone’, and we take that pretty seriously. On the field, it means competitive, world-class cricket for the dedicated cricket fan. Off the field, it really means a great social occasion for people to come and enjoy the atmosphere, the music and a day out with friends and family.If I have to say what I want fans to take away, it's that we do hear you, we do listen to what you want, and we will always strive to deliver based on the feedback that fans are giving us.
Article Summary: Lynn Naudé, COO of SA20, talks to TOI about the league's rapid rise. SA20 has established itself as one of the most prominent T20 leagues outside the IPL. COO says league's success has been down to getting the fundamentals right. He talks about securing a prime South African summer window.

The SA20 Season 5 auction will see 156 cricketers go under the hammer on October 7, with former Joburg Super Kings captain Faf du Plessis Rassie van der Dussen and all-rounder Wiaan Mulder among the leading South African names available.The shortlist was trimmed down from 789 players who initially registered for the auction. Fast bowler Matthew Boast, who commanded the joint-highest bid at the Season 2 auction, is among the players in this category, alongside former South Africa Under-19 captain Jason Rowles.The first four SA20 auctions have produced several significant deals. Tristan Stubbs fetched $554,693 at the inaugural auction, while Dewald Brevis set a new record with a $994,834 deal last season.The auction has also provided a route for several South African players to gain exposure to international franchise cricket, with some subsequently securing further opportunities on the global T20 circuit.The overseas contingent includes former West Indies captain Kieron Pollard, New Zealand pacer Trent Boult, Shimron Hetmyer, Shamar Joseph, Mohammad Nabi, AM Ghazanfar, Jordan Cox, Aneurin Donald, Rehan Ahmed and Richard Gleeson.Several established T20 names are already part of the six franchises, including Jos Buttler, Joe Root, Sam Curran, Sunil Narine, Kane Williamson, Andre Russell, Sherfane Rutherford, Mitchell Marsh and Phil Salt.The auction will be broadcast live on SuperSport at 5pm SAST, JioStar at 8.30pm IST, Sky Sports at 4pm BST, Apex at 7.30pm PKT, Fox Sports at 11pm AEDT and Willow TV at 11am ET. Article Title: ‘Preparation is important’: Abhishek Sharma explains how he stays ahead of opposition bowlers
Article Text:
India's Abhishek Sharma (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

INDORE: Abhishek Sharma likes to do "uncomfortable" things during practice sessions. He believes that such preparation keeps him battle-ready and ensures he is not caught by "surprise" when facing world-class bowlers.With Roston Chase having dismissed the left-hander twice earlier in the series, and Abhishek's weakness against off-spinners well documented, West Indies began with the 34-year-old offie in an attempt to counter him from the word go.The 26-year-old knew what the visitors were trying to exploit, but this time he was ready. He bided his time, played out the first over he faced from Chase and, once settled, launched into him in the next. A 111.6 kmph faster one was smashed through the covers for four while a much slower delivery was deposited over wide long-off for six, and the dose was repeated as he struck another six over covers.Abhishek never looked back thereafter as he raced to his 14th T20I fifty and finished with a 30-ball 69. During his innings at the Holkar Stadium on Sunday, he achieved another staggering feat, scoring 72 per cent of his runs through the off-side.In the process, he became the fastest batter to score 2,000 T20I runs. He reached the landmark in just 1,024 balls, 140 fewer than the previous record holder, Suryakumar Yadav , who took 1,164 deliveries to get there.Abhishek's career strike rate stands at 195.95, and he feels the preparation he puts in behind the scenes is crucial to sustaining that approach."I think preparation is important. If I want to just continue playing like this, and that's the plan for the team, then preparation really matters. I always believe in that. It always depends on the teams and the bowlers I'm going to face. So, whenever I have time, it's (preparation) very specific... how bowlers are going to plan against me, how I'm going to execute my plan and dominate," said Abhishek."As a batter, if you have to face world-class bowlers, you have to be ready for all the plans. I always want that preparation in practice which makes me a bit uncomfortable so that I wouldn't be surprised in the match. So I always allow myself to be in that position during training," he added.West Indies allrounder Shamar Springer also lauded Abhishek's innings, which circumvented their plans and forced them to switch to a 'Plan B' that involved bowling a defensive line to him."He is a world-class player. But I guess our 'Plan B' was to just be as defensive as possible and try to make him get singles and twos. It was just a matter of trying to pull him back because there's not much control you can really have here. The wickets are so good and those players are world-class players and they're the best for a reason. So, it's not really much you can do besides be defensive," said Springer.Earlier in the year, during the T20 World Cup, Abhishek struggled against off-spinners and almost every team targeted that weakness. During that period, he would often try to force his way out of trouble.Eight months later, while Abhishek's ability to destroy attacks at the top remains intact, his willingness to wait just a little longer before launching into the opposition has made this version of him an even scarier proposition for opponents to dismantle.
Article Summary: India's Abhishek Sharma became the fastest batter to score 2,000 T20I runs. He reached the landmark in just 1,024 balls, 140 fewer than the previous record holder, Suryakumar Yadav. He scored 72 per cent of his runs through the off-side during his innings at the Holkar Stadium.

NEW DELHI: India fast bowler Prince Yadav made a valuable contribution with the bat in the third T20I against the West Indies in Indore. After India's 14-run victory, Prince revealed that he had used Abhishek Sharma 's bat to score his quick runs.Prince hit three fours in the final over bowled by Shamar Joseph to finish with 13 runs off six balls. His cameo helped India post 223/5 in 20 overs at the Holkar Stadium.Prince also impressed with the ball, giving away only 20 runs in his two overs during the death overs, when the West Indies needed more than 15 runs per over.Prince revealed that Abhishek had lent him his bat before his innings and had also given him a warning."Obviously, brother, it is great to contribute to the team, whether it's with the ball, bat, or in the fielding. The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) has shifted ongoing President’s Trophy Grade 1 matches away from Peshawar and Abbottabad following the federal government’s announcement of a state of emergency and the imposition of governor’s rule in the politically troubled province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.The venue changes come amid escalating political tensions involving the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of former prime minister Imran Khan , which had been governing the province. According to a Cricinfo report, the PCB has moved fixtures originally scheduled at Imran Khan Stadium in Peshawar and Abbottabad Cricket Stadium to venues in Sheikhupura and Lahore.The decision has disrupted the schedule as the first-class competition approaches the end of its league stage. Matches in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, the other two host cities, will continue as planned.The emergency was announced following presidential approval of recommendations submitted by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ’s federal cabinet. The political developments also led to the detention of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and some members of his cabinet, according to Pakistan’s junior interior minister Talal Chaudhry, who confirmed the detentions to Reuters.Under the revised schedule, Ghani will face Hyderabad Kingsmen Academy at Rana Naveed Academy in Sheikhupura from October 14. The match between Sui Northern Gas Pipelines Limited (SNGPL) and Oil and Gas Development Company Limited (OGDCL) has been moved to the LCCA Ground in Lahore, adjacent to Gaddafi Stadium, with the fixture also beginning on October 14.The current round is the penultimate one of the league stage, with the sixth round beginning on Monday. The PCB has also pushed back the final round by a day, with matches now scheduled to begin on October 19.The revised schedule includes further changes to the tournament’s closing fixtures. Lahore’s LCCA Ground will host the final-round encounter between Markhor IT Solutions and Pakistan TV.In Islamabad, Hyderabad Kingsmen Academy will take on State Bank of Pakistan at the National Cricket Ground, while the Diamond Club ground will continue to serve as another venue in the capital.The venue changes come as the PCB has sought to expand domestic cricket beyond its traditional centres. Abbottabad has regularly hosted first-class fixtures, while Peshawar’s Imran Khan Stadium returned to the senior men’s domestic calendar last season after nearly seven years away, hosting nine Quaid-e-Azam Trophy matches following renovation work.Peshawar had also been allocated its first Pakistan Super League match this year. However, the PSL was eventually restricted to Lahore and Karachi amid federal fuel-conservation measures introduced following the West Asia crisis.The latest changes underline how the political situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has affected the domestic cricket calendar, forcing the PCB to relocate fixtures during a crucial phase of the competition.
Article Summary: PCB revises venues as political tensions escalate. Final-round fixtures also affected by the changes. Decision disrupted the schedule as the first-class competition approaches the end of its league stage. Matches in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, the other two host cities, will continue as planned.

NEW DELHI: India vice-captain Tilak Varma may have endured an unusual run-out in the third T20I against West Indies, but the match also brought a significant personal milestone for the left-handed batter. Tilak became only the fifth Indian fielder to complete 50 catches in T20Is during Sunday's match in Indore, joining an elite list featuring Rohit Sharma, Hardik Pandya, Suryakumar Yadav and Virat Kohli What makes Tilak's achievement particularly impressive is the efficiency with which he has reached the landmark. His 50 catches have come in just 68 T20I appearances, giving him a dismissals-per-innings ratio of 0.757 — the best among Indian fielders with at least 50 outfield catches in the format.Globally, Tilak's ratio is second only to the United Arab Emirates' Muhammad Waseem, who has taken 76 catches in 99 outings at a ratio of 0.767. Among the 34 players to have taken at least 50 outfield catches in men's T20Is, only Waseem has a better ratio.Tilak's achievement places him alongside some of India's most accomplished fielders in the shortest format. Rohit leads the list with 65 catches, followed by Hardik with 64, Suryakumar with 58 and Kohli with 54.Reaching the milestone in just 68 appearances underlines Tilak's contribution in the field, with his catches-per-innings record placing him among the most efficient outfielders in men's T20I cricket.The milestone came during a match in which Tilak was also involved in an unusual dismissal. Batting in the 17th over, he and Axar Patel appeared to believe that West Indies fielder Kamil Pooran had touched the boundary rope while stopping a shot off Gudakesh Motie.The pair completed a single and exchanged a fist bump, assuming the ball would be called a four. But Pooran had kept the ball in play and returned it quickly. Axar made his ground at the striker's end, while Tilak continued towards his crease, seemingly unaware of the situation. Motie collected the ball and broke the stumps at the bowler's end, with the third umpire confirming the run-out.Tilak departed for 28 off 16 balls, including four boundaries. India, however, recovered to post 223, powered by Abhishek Sharma's 69 off 30 balls, and went on to beat West Indies by 14 runs.Arshdeep Singh claimed three wickets and Naman Dhir took two as West Indies finished on 209/7. The victory gave India a 2-1 lead in the five-match series.
Article Summary: Tilak Varma becomes fifth Indian fielder to complete 50 catches in T20Is. His 50 catches have come in just 68 T20I appearances, giving him a dismissals-per- innings ratio of 0.757. Rohit Sharma leads the list with 65 catches, followed by Hardik with 64, Suryakumar with 58 and Virat Kohli with 54.

Article Title: India vs West Indies: ‘Plan B’ against Abhishek Sharma revealed! India star says he knew West Indies’ strategy
Article Text:
Abhishek Sharma (Pic credit: BCCI)

India stay ruthless despite late scare

NEW DELHI: India opener Abhishek Sharma knew the West Indies had a plan to contain him. His response was simple: play better than their plan.The left-hander’s explosive 30-ball 69 proved decisive as India defeated the West Indies by 14 runs in the third T20I to take a 2-1 lead in the five-match series. West Indies all-rounder Shamar Springer later revealed that the visitors’ Plan B against the in-form opener was to adopt a defensive approach and restrict him to singles and twos rather than allow him to continue his big-hitting spree.Abhishek smashed six fours and five sixes, recording his 14th T20I half-century and becoming the fastest player to reach 2,000 runs in the format in terms of balls faced. His 108-run partnership with Ishan Kishan , who scored 37, helped India post 223 before the bowlers held their nerve to restrict the visitors to 209/7.With Abhishek initially taking on Roston Chase’s off-spin, the West Indies had to reconsider their approach against the dangerous opener. Springer explained that the team decided to focus on damage control rather than attempt an aggressive dismissal.“He is a world-class player. Kudos to him, for sure. But I guess our plan B is to just be as defensive as possible and try to make him get singles and twos, running at moments. Nothing too extravagant,” Springer told reporters after the match.“It was just a matter of trying to pull him back and be as impressive as possible.Because there's not much control you can really have here. The wickets are so good and those players are world-class players and they're the best for a reason. So, it's not really much you can really do besides be defensive,” he added.The strategy, however, could not prevent Abhishek from giving India a flying start. The opener’s assault provided the home side with the cushion they needed to withstand a late West Indies charge.Springer himself threatened to turn the contest around with an unbeaten 35 off just 11 balls, including four sixes and two fours, but the visitors eventually fell 14 runs short.Abhishek acknowledged that the West Indies’ tactics against him were on his mind, particularly when Chase opened the bowling and the field was set to challenge his preferred scoring areas.“I wouldn't say it was deliberate, but it was there in my mind that they had a plan against me,” Abhishek said.“(With the) off-spinner bowling against me, it was just a battle between him and me. I gave him respect in the first over because he is bowling really well in this series, so it is just the plan that went pretty well for me as well.”The opener, however, insisted that his strokeplay was dictated by the field rather than any premeditated attempt to target a particular area.“...because in the powerplay, I was trying to just get a few runs and they had a plan for me, and I had to play better than that,” he said. “I don't think and play deliberately. It just happens when I see the field placement, whenever they have a field placement which allows me to just give myself room and play those shots.”Abhishek said India were determined not to let the West Indies back into the contest, knowing the visitors possessed enough batting firepower to threaten even in difficult situations.“West Indies is such a team that you can never say that the match is now on our side,” he said, recalling how the opposition’s batters had shown their ability to change the course of a game.“That was in our mind because we saw in the last match that whichever batsman comes in, (with) the conditions that we have here, it is very easy for them to take the match to their side.”“So that was in our mind even when we were losing wickets, we were saying that we would be ruthless thereon and we will not give them a single chance to come back,” Abhishek added.Springer felt the West Indies could have taken the chase closer, pointing to missed scoring opportunities and the pitch playing lower than expected. He also credited the Indian bowlers for using the conditions effectively.India’s 14-run victory gave them a 2-1 series lead, with Abhishek’s early onslaught once again underlining why opposition sides are searching for ways to contain him.
Article Summary: India beat West Indies by 14 runs in third T20I to take 2-1 lead in five-match series. West Indies all-rounder Shamar Springer reveals visitors' Plan B against Abhishek Sharma. Springer: 'Our plan B is to just be as defensive as possible and try to make him get singles'

MUMBAI: Siddhesh Lad carried last season’s rich form into the new one, playing a captain’s hand to rescue Mumbai on a testing opening day of their Elite Group D Ranji Trophy match against Chandigarh at the Wankhede Stadium on Sunday.Lad, Mumbai’s dependable crisis man, remained unbeaten on 80 off 176 balls, with eight fours, as the hosts reached 249/5 at stumps after being asked to bat first.The 34-year-old, who was Mumbai’s highest run-getter in the 2025-26 Ranji Trophy with 774 runs in eight matches, spent 255 minutes at the crease and completed 5,000 first-class runs for Mumbai on his first day as captain.Mumbai were in trouble at 144/4 in the 57th over after Sarfaraz Khan fell for 1 shortly before tea. Lad then added 40 for the fifth wicket with wicketkeeper-batter Akash Anand, who made 22 off 36 balls.After Anand was caught at slip off left-arm spinner Nishunk Birla, Lad found another steady partner in Shams Mulani. The pair added an unbroken 68 off 98 balls for the sixth wicket, with Mulani unbeaten on 27.Lad reached his 31st first-class half-century off 135 balls and is now closing in on his 16th first-class hundred.Mumbai were hit early when India Test opener Yashasvi Jaiswal fell for a 13-ball duck, edging Jagjit Singh to second slip in the third over.Sarfaraz was later adjudged lbw to pacer Nikhil Dhanda while shouldering arms. The decision left him visibly unhappy.Sarfaraz’s wicket came soon after Musheer Khan was caught behind off Dhanda, giving Chandigarh two key breakthroughs in successive overs. Dhanda finished the day as the pick of the bowlers with 3/44 in 15 overs. Musheer had earlier made a patient 65 off 149 balls, with four fours. He and vice-captain Ayush Mhatre rebuilt the innings after Jaiswal’s early dismissal, adding 76 for the second wicket in 145 balls.Mhatre showed more enterprise during his 48 off 82 balls, hitting seven fours and a six, before Dhanda bowled him with one that came back in. Musheer and Lad then added 65 for the third wicket.Mumbai head coach Omkar Salvi praised Lad’s commitment to red-ball cricket and his influence on younger players.“I think it’s his passion to play red-ball cricket. He is very passionate about it, which helps him and the team. The way he guides the younger players, his calmness, it enables them to express themselves,” Salvi said after the day’s play. “Over the last two seasons, the way Siddhesh has grown as a player, you can see his leadership qualities. His calm demeanour at the crease brings calmness to the dressing room. He has seen highs and lows, so he is a very settled player now. He uses his experience very well, and it helps the team.”
Article Summary: Siddhesh Lad unbeaten on 80 off 176 balls, with eight fours, as Mumbai reach 249/5 at stumps. The 34-year-old was Mumbai’s highest run-getter in the 2025-26 Ranji Trophy with 774 runs in eight matches. Lad completed 5,000 first-class runs for Mumbai on his first day as captain.

Article Title: How Neeraj Chopra's javelin helped Rohit Yadav win Asian Games bronze
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: When Rohit Yadav stepped onto the field in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, for the Asian Games javelin final, he carried more than a piece of sporting equipment. In his hand was a signed javelin belonging to Olympic and world champion Neeraj Chopra — a quiet gesture of support that would accompany him to an international podium.The story began in June, when Yadav struck gold at the National Inter State Senior Athletics Championships in Bhubaneswar with a personal best of 87.05m. Upon returning to his training base in NIS Patiala, he discovered that his preferred javelin had bent, apparently during air transit in its protective PVC tube in the aircraft’s cargo hold.Yadav subsequently competed at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow with a borrowed implement, finishing seventh with 81.56m in cold, windy conditions. With the Asian Games approaching, he faced the prospect of competing without his trusted javelin.“For the Asian Games, I didn’t have my own javelin. My preferred one was damaged and had bent. While coming to Delhi from Patiala for the Indian Athletics Final Series on Sept 10, I spoke to Neeraj bhai,” Yadav told TOI.“We have been in regular touch. I knew he had returned to India for rehabilitation. I told him I didn’t have a javelin of my own for the Asian Games.He immediately came to my rescue and sent me one of his signed javelins through a private taxi service to the Jawaharlal Nehru (JLN) stadium,” he added.Chopra had withdrawn from the remainder of the season, including the Asian Games, to recover from an ankle ligament injury. His absence left India without its two-time defending champion, but his gesture ensured that a fellow Indian thrower had the equipment he needed.There was, however, a catch. Yadav could not use the javelin in Delhi because it had not been registered with the Technical Information Centre (TIC) for inspection. He borrowed another registered implement for the event, then carefully packed Chopra’s gift for Japan.“At the Asian Games, I registered two javelins with the TIC. But I used the one Neeraj bhai gave me. I had a good grip and hold over it, and with that javelin I made the winning throw to secure bronze with 84.35m,” he said.“I will remain thankful to Neeraj bhai. I have kept that javelin with me and will use it in future competitions as well.”After his competition, Rohit listened to Chopra’s congratulatory voice message.“He told me to enjoy the win and savour my first big international medal. He said that when he returns fully fit, we will compete together, and that I have a long way to go.”Back home in Uttar Pradesh’s Jaunpur, Yadav is taking the off-season to spend time with family until Diwali.“I want to earn a Diamond League entry, compete internationally and qualify for the World Championships next year. The ultimate target remains the Los Angeles Olympics,” he added.
Article Summary: Rohit Yadav won bronze at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. Yadav used a signed javelin belonging to Olympic and world champion Neeraj Chopra. Chopra had withdrawn from the remainder of the season to recover from an ankle ligament injury.

Article Title: ‘Olympic gold jeetna hai’: Kumkum Mohod’s big dream after ending Korea’s stranglehold in archery at Asian Games 2026
Article Text:
Kumkum Mohod

TimesofIndia.com

Kumkum Mohod

Manifestation: ‘I had been visualising this for a year’

Kumkum Mohod (AP Photo)

Road to the final: Learning from the best, then beating her

‘My family always supported me’

Gold medallist India's Kumkum Anil Mohod, Ankita Bhakat and Kirti celebrate on the podium during the victory ceremony. (Reuters Photo)

Beyond archery: Drawing, crafts and a dream before sleep

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The ultimate dream: Olympic gold

(Credit: Special arrangement)

NEW DELHI: For years, Kumkum Mohod had watched South Korean archers closely, studying their technique and trying to understand what made them so dominant in recurve archery. She observed their movements, learnt from their approach and looked at the qualities that had made them role models for young Indian archers like her.But when the 17-year-old stood on the shooting line at the Asian Games , just seconds away from releasing her arrow, she had a message for herself: the Koreans were not unbeatable.“Maine match shuru hone se khud ko bol diya tha, woh 10 maarte hain, to mujhe bhi 10 hi maarna hai [I told myself before the match began: they shoot 10s too, so I have to shoot 10s as well],” Asian Games 2026 gold medallist archer Kumkum Mohod toldin an exclusive interview.The 17-year-old made history by winning the women’s individual recurve gold at the Asian Games, beating the Republic of Korea’s Oh Yejin in the final.In doing so, she ended South Korea’s hold on the individual recurve gold at the Games and helped India secure a quota place for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.Before leaving for Aichi-Nagoya, Kumkum had already imagined herself standing on the top of the podium.She had also visualised beating her inspiration, South Korea’s Kang Chaeyoung, whom she eventually defeated in the quarterfinals on her way to the historic gold.Kumkum became the first Indian to win an individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. She also won gold in the women’s recurve team event and silver in the mixed team event with Dhiraj Bommadevara, finishing the Games with three medals.“Until now, no one had managed to do it. But we Indians have done it. We have put the Koreans on a pedestal, as if they are the only ones who can do it and hit those scores. Before the match began, I told myself that they shoot 10s too, and we have to shoot 10s as well,” she said.For Kumkum, the feeling of becoming an Asian Games champion is still sinking in. The young archer said the result did not come as a complete surprise because she had been visualising the moment for a year, even before she stepped onto the field in Japan.For a year leading up to the Asian Games, she repeated the same words five times before going to sleep: “Kumkum, Asian Games gold jeetna hai” (Kumkum, you have to win Asian Games gold). She would then say “Hare Krishna”, reflecting her devotion to Lord Krishna.Her belief was tested against some of the world's best archers. Kumkum defeated South Korea’s reigning world champion and Olympic medallist Kang Chaeyoung 6-3 in the quarterfinals before beating China’s Zhu Jingyi 6-2 in the semifinals.In the final, she held her nerve against South Korea’s Oh Yejin. The contest ended 5-5 after five sets, forcing a shoot-off. Oh shot an eight, while Kumkum hit a 10 to seal the gold medal.Kumkum had been trailing during the match and needed to win the fifth set to stay in contention. She responded by shooting a perfect 30 to force the shoot-off before producing the decisive 10.“The final went really well. I was trailing, but I remained strong. I believed in myself and knew I could do it because I had been visualising this for the past year. I kept imagining that I would face Kang in a match and that it would be a final,” Kumkum said.When Oh shot an eight in the shoot-off, Kumkum had to focus on her own shot rather than the possibility of winning. She knew she had to deliver, regardless of what her opponent had scored.“I had made up my mind that day that I had to prove myself. My first thought was, ‘Kumkum, you still have to shoot a good shot.’ Even if she had shot a 10, I was very confident at that moment,” she said.“I enjoyed that moment while shooting. There is always some pressure, but I tried to reduce it. Anyone who says there is no pressure is absolutely wrong. Sport is about nerves and thrilling moments. There is always adrenaline, and you have to overcome it. The person who manages to do that wins,” she said.Kumkum's journey to the gold medal included victories over some of the world's leading archers. But one of the most memorable moments for her was beating Kang, an archer she had admired and learnt from since the beginning of her career.Kang had been Kumkum's inspiration because of her technique, focus, composure and ability to deliver under pressure. Kumkum paid particular attention to her release and follow-through, as well as the way she maintained her technique in crucial moments.At the Asian Games, however, the young Indian found herself competing against the very archer she had looked up to for years - and came out on top.“Kang’s shooting technique is very good. Her release is excellent, and she does not drop her bow after the follow-through. Her shooting is very strong,” Kumkum said.So, the victory carried special meaning. After the match, Kumkum exchanged a high-five with her opponent and told her, “Good shooting, good shooting.”Kang smiled and congratulated her.“I have learnt a lot from her, and I was happy. She is a legend of the sport. She has made her country proud by winning medals, and now I have done the same. I am proud that I have made my country proud,” Kumkum said.Behind Kumkum’s success is a family that continued to believe in her, even when her performances were not going as planned.Her father, Anil Mohod, runs a business making sweet boxes. As Kumkum was good at academics, her father initially wanted her to focus on her studies. But when he saw her growing interest in archery, her family supported her sporting ambitions while ensuring that she did not neglect her education.Kumkum is the couple’s only child and is currently in Class 12.“I joined archery, and within six months, I won a medal. After that, I learnt about the Olympics and understood what the sport could lead to. I also learnt that India had not won a medal in this event. My interest grew, and I started working harder,” she said.Her family’s faith in her remained strong even during difficult periods.“When I was not doing well, my family told me that I could do it. They have supported me a lot, and I never faced any problems because of them,” she said.Now, following her historic achievement, the Mohod household has been welcoming a steady stream of visitors. Neighbours, friends, relatives, sports associations and fellow sportspersons have been arriving to congratulate the family.Kumkum said the celebrations have kept everyone busy, with little time to rest.“It feels like a wedding atmosphere at home. People keep coming and going, and we are hardly getting any sleep. All thanks to Krishna ji,” she said.Away from the archery range, Kumkum enjoys spending time with a paintbrush and a colour palette. Drawing and craftwork are among her favourite hobbies, giving her a break from the demands of training and competition.“I like drawing and crafting. I also enjoy making things with my hands,” she said.She also enjoys watching television shows and films. Her favourites include Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah and sports-based films such as Dangal, Mary Kom, Ghoomer and Bhaag Milkha Bhaag.Unlike many teenagers, Kumkum has never had Facebook or Instagram accounts. She also disabled YouTube a few months before the Asian Games. Drawing, craftwork and reading are among the activities she enjoys away from the range.“I never had Facebook or Instagram. I also disabled YouTube a few months before the Asian Games. My crafts, drawing and reading books help me a lot,” she said.Kumkum has already achieved a major milestone by winning three medals at the Asian Games and helping India secure a quota place for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. But she has a bigger dream — winning India's first Olympic gold medal in archery.The words she repeated before going to sleep for a year - “Kumkum, Asian Games gold jeetna hai” - now reflect a new ambition: “Kumkum, Olympic gold jeetna hai.”At home, a small message on the wall serves as a reminder of what she wants to achieve.“LA 2028 gold is the target. That is the dream. I do not want to think too far ahead just yet, but that is the target. I will work hard for it and strengthen myself mentally,” Kumkum signed off.
Article Summary: Kumkum Mohod is the first Indian to win an individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. The 17-year-old made history by beating the Republic of Korea’s Oh Yejin in the final. She also won gold in the women's recurvies team event and silver in the mixed team event.

Article Title: Historic Olympic quota, multiple medals — but no salary: India’s compound archery coach unhappy over payment delay
Article Text:
Sahil Jadhav, left, and Chikitha Taniparthi, right, celebrate with coach Dave Cousins after winning the compound mixed team archery gold. (PTI Photo)

A historic breakthrough, but a salary dispute

Sahil Jadhav and Chikitha Taniparthi with team coach Dave Cousins during the Asian Games. (PTI Photo)

AAI, SAI say payment will be cleared soon

Building towards LA 2028

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India's compound archers made history at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games by becoming the first nation to secure an Olympic quota in the discipline. But while the team celebrated a landmark achievement and a rich medal haul, the foreign coach who helped guide them to success was left unhappy over a salary delay stretching beyond three months.American Dave Cousins, appointed as India's chief compound archery coach in May, is learnt to have threatened to quit and leave the country if his pending dues were not cleared, as per a PTI report.The development has raised questions about the support extended to a coach who has already delivered significant results as India builds towards the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. However, the Archery Association of India (AAI) and the Sports Authority of India (SAI) have acknowledged the delay, attributing it to a technical issue and saying the matter has now been resolved, with the payment expected to be cleared shortly."He has spoken to some officials and said if the dues are not cleared he's leaving home. He's really unhappy with the way he's been treated for three months... he's not been paid so far," sources told PTI.Cousins helped India win three gold medals and a bronze in compound archery at the Asian Games, contributing to the country's overall haul of five gold, two silver and two bronze across recurve and compound events.The biggest breakthrough came in the mixed-team event, where the relatively unfancied Indian pair of Sahil Jadhav and Chikitha Taniparthi stunned South Korea in a shoot-off after the final was tied 157-157 over four ends.The victory secured India its first-ever Olympic quota in compound archery, a discipline that will feature a mixed-team event at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.Cousins had taken charge of India's compound programme with the responsibility of building a competitive unit for the Olympics. His results at the Asian Games came with a group that had faced questions about its ability to deliver at the highest level.The American had also guided 18-year-old Prithika Pradeep to her maiden World Cup bronze at the Madrid stage in Spain.Reflecting on India's Asian Games campaign, Cousins had stressed that preparation, rather than medal predictions, was the team's priority."The only thing we were willing to commit to is that our athletes would go prepared and that they would execute the process as best they could," he had said."When the training is right, the preparation is right and the ecosystem is right, these are the results you get. We're exceptionally happy to clinch the first-ever compound archery spot for the Olympic Games. That's a huge thing for us right now."AAI treasurer Dr Joris Paulose Ummacheril acknowledged the delay but said the issue had been resolved and the payment would be made shortly."There was some issue with the Sports Authority of India (SAI), so the payment got delayed. But it has all been worked out, and it will be paid within two days," Joris told PTI.An SAI official in New Delhi also attributed the delay to a technical problem involving the bank, adding that the matter was being processed."We have already spoken to him and assured him that the payment is under process. It got delayed because of a technical issue with the bank, and it should be done within a couple of days," the official said.The assurances suggest that the dispute could be resolved soon, although the episode has highlighted the administrative challenges that can undermine the momentum generated by sporting success.Cousins, 49, is a former world No. 1 who won World Archery Championship titles in 1999 and 2003. His appointment in May followed the departure of Sergio Pagni, under whom India swept all five archery gold medals at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou.Meanwhile, the federation is also in talks with South Korean coach Park Chae-soon to take charge of India's recurve programme ahead of LA 2028. Park, who coached South Korea's women's team at the London 2012 Olympics and men's team at Rio 2016, is expected to join by December.With India's archers building momentum towards the next Olympics, Cousins' contribution has already produced a landmark result in compound archery. The historic quota and multiple Asian Games medals have strengthened India's prospects in a discipline making its Olympic debut in Los Angeles.
Article Summary: India's compound archers made history at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games by becoming the first nation to secure an Olympic quota in the discipline. Coach Dave Cousins is learnt to have threatened to quit and leave the country if his pending dues were not cleared. The development has raised questions about the support extended to a coach who has already delivered significant results as India builds towards the 2028 Olympics.

Article Title: ‘I was a daughter of Himachal’: Ritu Negi’s heartbreak after home state drops Asian Games gold medallist from Rs 1 crore reward list
Article Text:
Indian women's Kabaddi player Ritu Negi. (ANI Photo)

‘Why is Himachal Pradesh behaving this way at this stage of my career?’

India women's kabaddi team after winning the Asian Games gold medal in Japan.

Her father asks: Does a daughter stop belonging to her state after marriage?

Why three kabaddi players were awarded Rs 1 crore each

Government promises to review the decision

Another gold medal, but a different kind of disappointment

Former India captain Ritu Negi has represented the country at three consecutive Asian Games, won two gold medals and a silver, and led the women's kabaddi team to the top of the podium at the 2023 edition in Hangzhou. Yet, after being part of India's gold-medal-winning squad again at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, the Arjuna Awardee has found herself at the centre of an unexpected controversy in her home state of Himachal Pradesh.Negi's name was missing from the state's list of athletes announced for a cash reward of Rs 1 crore following India's women's kabaddi triumph in Japan. The decision has left the veteran player disappointed and raised questions about whether an accomplished sportsperson should lose recognition from her home state simply because she is married in another state.Negi hails from the Shillai region of Sirmaur district but is married in Panipat, Haryana. The omission has been particularly difficult to understand because she received a cash reward from Himachal Pradesh after India's women's kabaddi team won gold at the 2023 Asian Games, when she was the captain.This time, however, her name was left out while three other players from the state were included in the reward list."Until a week ago, I was a daughter of Himachal and the CM shared a congratulatory message on Facebook, while former CM Jairam Thakur and Member of Parliament Anurag Thakur had called to congratulate me," Negi told the media while expressing her displeasure."I simply cannot understand what changed so suddenly two days ago."The decision to exclude Negi has struck a particularly sensitive chord because of her long association with Indian kabaddi and her contribution to the state's sporting reputation.The veteran has represented India at three consecutive Asian Games, winning two gold medals and a silver. She captained the women's team to gold at Hangzhou in 2023 and remained part of the squad that successfully defended the title in Japan.India edged past Iran 37-34 in a tense final at the Aichi-Nagoya Games, holding on to its advantage in the closing stages to secure another Asian Games gold.The achievement should have been another moment of pride for the player and her home state. Instead, the omission from the reward list has left Negi questioning the recognition being extended to her.She pointed out that although she is employed by Indian Railways , she has consistently represented Himachal Pradesh, rather than Haryana, in domestic competitions."Why Himachal Pradesh is behaving in such a way at this stage of my career?" she asked.For Negi, the issue goes beyond the financial incentive. It is about recognition for years of representing India and maintaining her sporting association with the state from which she hails.Negi's father, Bhavan Singh Negi, has also questioned the decision, asking whether a daughter ceases to belong to her home state simply because she gets married elsewhere.Speaking from Shillai in Sirmaur district, he pointed out that his daughter had received a cash reward from the Himachal government after the 2023 Asian Games, despite being married in Haryana.That precedent has made the latest omission even harder for the family to comprehend. They believe marriage should not erase an athlete's roots or diminish her contribution to the state she continues to represent in domestic competitions.The controversy has since drawn reactions from political leaders and people associated with sports in Himachal Pradesh.The debate has consequently become about more than a reward announced after a sporting achievement. It has raised questions about how states recognise athletes who continue to bring them distinction despite changes in their personal circumstances.The controversy emerged after Himachal Pradesh Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu announced a cash reward of Rs 1 crore each for three players from the state who were part of India's women's kabaddi gold-medal-winning squad at the Aichi-Nagoya Games.The recipients were Pushpa Rana, Jyoti Thakur and Bhawna Thakur. Indian women's cricket player Renuka Thakur was also announced as a recipient of Rs 1 crore in recognition of her achievements.The announcement followed an earlier disagreement over the amount offered to the kabaddi players. Initially, the three players had been informed that they would receive Rs 33 lakh each, a figure they felt was below their entitlement under the state's sports policy. They subsequently met Sukhu to raise their concerns over the cash incentives and employment opportunities.Pushpa Rana said the players were disappointed by the original announcement."Look, we were very disappointed because according to the sports policy, we were not being given the amount that was due to us. So literally, anyone would be disappointed," she told IANS.Following the meeting, the Chief Minister assured the players that the reward would be increased to Rs 1 crore each. The state government also announced government employment for the three kabaddi players, with options in the police department or the Youth Services and Sports Department.While the revised announcement addressed the players' concerns over the amount, Negi's omission from the list brought a fresh controversy into focus.The Himachal Pradesh government has not publicly provided a definitive explanation for why Negi's name was removed from the list.Sports Minister Yadvinder Goma said he was unaware of the reason behind the change and would examine the file before discussing the matter with the Chief Minister.Meanwhile, sources in the state government indicated that officials were monitoring the Haryana government's position on the matter. They suggested that Himachal Pradesh could consider a decision later, particularly since Haryana had not yet announced a cash award for Negi.The sources also indicated that her employment with Indian Railways was not a factor in the matter.The distinction is important because Negi has maintained that she has continued to represent Himachal Pradesh in domestic competitions despite her marriage and employment outside the state.Whether the government ultimately revises its list remains to be seen. For now, the Sports Minister's assurance that he will review the matter offers a possible route towards resolving the dispute.For Negi, the timing of the controversy is especially poignant.At the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou, she captained the women's kabaddi side to gold and received recognition from her home state. At the Aichi-Nagoya Games, she again stood among the Indian players who helped defend the title, contributing to a campaign that ended with another gold medal for the country.Her sporting journey has been built around representing India at the highest level while continuing to identify with Himachal Pradesh. The latest controversy has placed that connection under an uncomfortable spotlight.Negi's case also highlights a broader challenge in Indian sport: ensuring that recognition for athletes reflects their achievements and contributions, rather than becoming entangled in questions about residence, marriage or administrative eligibility.The government has yet to make its final position clear, and the possibility of reconsideration remains open. Until then, the former India captain's disappointment stands as a reminder that recognition can matter as much as the reward itself.
